extracted.intended_audience: general public (educators, parents, students, researchers, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing definitions, types, characteristics, contexts, effects, prevention and response strategies for bullying across settings (schools, workplace, online, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying is the use of force, coercion, hurtful teasing, comments, or threats, in order to abuse, aggressively dominate, or intimidate one or more others. The behavior is often repeated and habitual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia emphasizes repetition and habitual nature; includes examples (teasing, threats) and notes bullying is a subcategory of aggressive behavior. The definition highlights intent to harm or dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential prerequisites / distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: One essential prerequisite is the perception (by the bully or by others) that an imbalance of physical or social power exists or is currently present. Bullying is characterized by hostile intent, the goal of addressing or attempting to 'fix' the imbalance of power, as well as repetition over a period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three features — power imbalance, hostile intent, and repetition — are presented as what distinguishes bullying from ordinary conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of bullying (basic classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying is divided into four basic types of abuse: psychological (sometimes referred to as 'emotional' or 'relational'), verbal, physical, and cyber (or 'electronic'), though an encounter can fall into more than one of these categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify incidents; note overlaps are common (e.g., relational + verbal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual bullying vs mobbing (group bullying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying can be performed individually or by a group, typically referred to as mobbing, in which the bully may have one or more followers who assist or reinforce the bully's behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobbing involves group dynamics (followers, positive feedback like laughing) and may require different interventions because of social reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical bullying behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical bullying is any bullying that physically harms someone's body or damages their possessions — examples include stealing, shoving, hitting, kicking, fighting, pantsing, and intentionally destroying someone's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical bullying often escalates over time and may be preceded by other forms; immediate intervention is recommended due to risk of injury or fatal outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal bullying behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal bullying includes derogatory name-calling and nicknaming, spreading rumors or lying, making threats, yelling in a rude or unkind tone, mocking someone's voice or style, laughing at someone, use of body language to torment, and making insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal bullying is one of the most common forms and often an early stage in bullying trajectories; it can be gendered in expression and subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational (social) bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Relational bullying (social aggression) uses relationships to hurt others — targeting reputation or social standing via social exclusion, slighting, or manipulation of friendships; it is often covert and can continue unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is less overt than physical bullying, relational bullying can persist longer; interventions should address social dynamics and reputation harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyberbullying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberbullying involves the use of technology (internet, email, messaging, social media, text) to harass, threaten, embarrass, or target another person; it is often more anonymous and may have legal consequences when adults are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key issues: online disinhibition effect (less accountability), permanence of online content, ease of reposting/sharing, and potential for wider audience — tailor prevention and response to platform dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobbing in workplaces and other settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobbing refers to bullying of an individual by a group in contexts such as family, peer group, school, workplace, neighborhood, or online; in workplaces it can involve rumor, innuendo, intimidation, humiliation, discrediting, and isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workplace mobbing is often labeled malicious harassment and may overlap with organizational culture issues; remedies may require organizational- and policy-level interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and motives of bullies
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives and traits associated with bullies include envy, resentment, arrogance, narcissism, shame, anxiety, depression, personality disorders, quickness to anger, addiction to aggressive behaviors, and concern with preserving self-image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research findings are mixed; some bullies have inflated but fragile egos or antisocial traits. Understanding motives can inform targeted interventions (e.g., mental health support, discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bystander behavior and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying often occurs in the presence of relatively uninvolved bystanders; the bystander effect can inhibit intervention. Bystanders who establish friendship or support groups are more likely to speak out, and interventions should increase self-efficacy and moral framing to encourage action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should focus on empowering bystanders, clarifying expectations to intervene, and building support structures; small opposing actions by bystanders can reduce bullying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim characteristics and vulnerability factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims often are physically and mentally weak, easily distraught, may have physical characteristics that make them targets, and commonly show low levels of self-esteem; victims of cyberbullying may differ in some self-esteem dimensions and sometimes use self-deprecating humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of vulnerability factors can help target prevention and support; note gendered patterns (boys more physical, girls more indirect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short- and long-term effects on targets and perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets of bullying can develop loneliness, depression, anxiety, low self-esteem, increased susceptibility to illness, maladjustment, eating disorders, body dysmorphia, and elevated suicide risk; perpetrators and victims both can show higher loneliness and other negative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of mental health risks to justify preventive programs and mental health services; suicide risk is elevated but bullying alone does not directly cause suicide — comorbid depression is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing bullying from normal peer conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying differs from normal peer conflict by being systematic/repeated, intentionally harmful, and involving a power differential where the aggressor holds more physical, social, or other power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educators and practitioners should distinguish developmental conflicts (which may promote social skills) from bullying that requires intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention strategies and programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying prevention is the collective effort to prevent, reduce and stop bullying; methods include teaching anti-bullying coping skills to children, carers and teachers, school-based programs, awareness events (Anti-Bullying Week, Day of Pink), and legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (e.g., 2019 study) suggests school-based programs may lower incidence (~25%); successful efforts often include education for trusted adults, teacher training (example: Media Heroes), and multi-stakeholder collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses and interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Address bullying early because ignoring it often allows it to worsen. Effective responses include intervention by trusted adults, talking to bullies about their behavior, empowering bystanders, and program collaborations in schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited emphasize early detection/intervention, parent/teacher involvement, and building programs that enable decreases in bullying after adult intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace bullying specific criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Workplace bullying occurs when an employee experiences a persistent pattern of mistreatment from others in the workplace that causes harm. It can be covert or overt and often involves someone in authority; bullies may operate within organizational rules and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions may need organizational policy changes, leadership training, reporting mechanisms, and recognition that workplace culture influences bullying prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal aspects and definitions across jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single legal definition globally: e.g., the UK has no legal definition of 'bullying', some US states have laws against it, and the UK Ministry of Defence defined bullying as 'the use of physical strength or the abuse of authority to intimidate or victimize others, or to give unlawful punishments'. Legal bullying can include vexatious legal actions (SLAPP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal recourse and definitions vary by jurisdiction; practitioners should consult local laws and precedents (e.g., negligence cases against school boards) when seeking remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contexts and settings of bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying can develop in any context where humans interact regularly: schools, families, workplaces, homes, neighborhoods, online platforms, colleges (ragging), military, prisons, healthcare, blue-collar jobs, IT, legal profession, and academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context shapes forms and remedies — e.g., online platforms require digital moderation strategies, while workplaces need organizational policy and leadership interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalizations and victim selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalizations for bullying include perceived differences (social class, race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, appearance, behavior, reputation, strength, size, ability). Bullies often select victims who are more available or vulnerable; members of minority groups may be more likely targeted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-bullying work should address prejudice and systemic factors that make some groups more vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of emotional intelligence (EI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower emotional intelligence appears to be related to involvement in bullying (as bully and/or victim); EI dimensions include perceiving, using, understanding, and managing emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EI is malleable, EI education is suggested as a component of prevention and intervention programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation with Dark Triad traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Research indicates bullying behavior is positively correlated with Dark Triad traits (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy), with psychopathy most strongly correlated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding personality correlates can inform risk assessment and tailored interventions, particularly where unprovoked aggression is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation pattern of bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical bullying is rarely the first form experienced; bullying often begins in verbal or relational forms and later progresses to physical violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early detection of verbal/relational bullying is critical to prevent escalation to physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online disinhibition and accountability issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The internet provides limited accountability and often no filter, creating an 'online disinhibition effect' that makes bullying feel easier and less restrictive; online content may persist indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital-literacy, moderation, and policies for content removal/sharing are important; consider long-term reputational consequences for targets.
